column2: On the authority of Abū Saʿīd Saʿd ibn Mālik ibn Sinān al-Khudrī (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) said: “There is to be no harm and no reciprocating harm.” A ḥasan hadith.

Reported by Ibn Mājah, al-Dāraquṭnī and others with a connected chain, and reported by Mālik in al-Muwaṭṭaʾ as mursal, from ʿAmr ibn Yaḥyā, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, omitting Abū Saʿīd. It has routes that strengthen one another.
Lā ḍarar (“no harm”): a man should not harm his brother by depriving him of anything of his right.
Wa-lā ḍirār (“and no reciprocating harm”): one should not repay the one who harmed him with more than an equal response and rightful redress.
There are other views on the explanation of “no harm and no reciprocating harm” which we will not prolong by mentioning.
Harm is to be removed. Many chapters of fiqh are built on this, such as returning goods for a defect and other things falling under this principle, which is taken from the hadith.

The prohibition of disposing of one's property in a way whose harm extends to others beyond the usual manner, such as lighting a fire on one's land on a windy day so that what is next to it burns; he has transgressed in doing so and is liable for compensation.
The prohibition of retaliating with more than the equivalent.
What Allah has commanded His servants is the very soundness of their religion and their worldly life,

and what He has forbidden them is the very corruption of their religion and their worldly life; He has not commanded them anything that harms them. That is why He lifted purification with water from the sick, and lifted the demand for repayment of a debt while the debtor is in hardship until he is at ease, and other things showing that our Sharīʿah is tolerant.
The printed text reads وعليك الضمان (“and you are liable”), evidently for وعليه الضمان (“and he is liable”).
